topics.title: Non-inverting amplifier and follower
topics.summary: Gain 1 + Rf/Rg with a very high input resistance; with Rf = 0 it becomes a unity-gain buffer.

lensNotes.circuit: The input goes straight into the op amp, so the source sees an almost infinite resistance. R_f and R_g feed back a fraction of the output; the gain is 1 + R_f/R_g, never below 1.
lensNotes.signals: No inversion: the output is an in-phase, scaled copy. With R_f = 0 it's a follower, a unity-gain buffer that isolates a signal source from its load.

prerequisiteNotes.opamp_ideal: The non-inverting amplifier uses the rule V− = V+: the op amp drives its output until the feedback divider hands back the input voltage.

goals: Find a non-inverting amplifier's output from Rf, Rg, and the input
Choose Rf and Rg from E-series values for a required gain, knowing the gain can never be below 1
Explain why the source sees a very high input resistance, and why a voltage follower isolates a source from its load
Predict what a heavier load or an Rf ten times larger does to the output, and explain why
topics.intuition: With negative feedback through the Rf–Rg divider, the op amp moves its output until the divider feeds exactly Vin back to the − input. The output is therefore Vin divided by the fraction Rg/(Rf + Rg), and the source drives only the + input, which draws no current (this holds only while the output stays inside its swing limits).
topics.why: The signal drives the + input, which draws no current, so the source is not loaded. Rf and Rg form a divider from the output to ground, with the − input at its midpoint. The − input draws no current either, so this divider is unloaded: V− = Vout·Rg/(Rf + Rg). Negative feedback drives V− to equal Vin, so Vout = Vin·(Rf + Rg)/Rg = Vin·(1 + Rf/Rg). A divider hands back at most all of its input, so the gain is at least 1. With Rf = 0 the fraction is 1, and the output follows the input.
topics.explanation: Start from the inverting amplifier and move the signal to the other input. The signal now goes straight to the + input. Rf runs from the output to the − input, and Rg from the − input to ground. They form a divider from the output. The − input draws no current, so the divider is unloaded. Negative feedback makes V− equal V+, which is the input. So the output must be the voltage whose divided-down share is Vin: Vout = Vin·(1 + Rf/Rg). The output is in phase with the input: no inversion. The gain is never below 1, because a divider cannot hand back more than it is given. The "1 +" is also why ten times Rf gives less than ten times the gain. The input resistance is very high: the source only drives the + input, which ideally takes no current. With Rf = 0 and Rg left out, the output connects straight to the − input: a voltage follower, gain 1. It passes on the voltage but not the load current: that comes from the op amp's supply, not from the source. The output still cannot go beyond its swing limits.

workedExample.problem: A sensor gives 0.80 V with no load and has a 10 kΩ output resistance. It drives a non-inverting amplifier on ±12 V supplies with Rf = 47 kΩ and Rg = 10 kΩ. Find the voltage at the + input, the gain, the output, and the largest sensor voltage before a rail-to-rail output clips. Then choose E24 resistors for a gain of 10 instead.
steps: The + input draws no current, so no current flows through the sensor's 10 kΩ and nothing is dropped across it: V+ = 0.80 V.
Vout = 0.80 V × 5.7 = 4.56 V, in phase with the input.

Check with the rules: the divider returns 4.56 V × 10 kΩ / (47 kΩ + 10 kΩ) = 0.80 V to the − input, equal to V+. The divider carries 4.56 V / 57 kΩ = 80 µA, supplied by the op amp's output, not by the sensor.
Clipping: 4.56 V is well inside ±12 V. A rail-to-rail output reaches +12 V when the input is 12 V / 5.7 = 2.11 V; an output that stops short of the rails clips earlier.

Compare: had the sensor driven an inverting stage with Rin = 10 kΩ and the same Rf = 47 kΩ, its 10 kΩ would sit in series with Rin: gain −47 kΩ / 20 kΩ = −2.35, half the −4.7 the resistors promise. The non-inverting stage does not load the sensor at all.

Gain of 10: Rf/Rg = 10 − 1 = 9. With Rg = 10 kΩ, Rf = 90 kΩ is not an E24 value; the nearest is 91 kΩ, giving 1 + 91 kΩ / 10 kΩ = 10.1, 1% high. Freeing Rg does better: 18 kΩ and 2.0 kΩ (or 27 kΩ and 3.0 kΩ) are both E24 with a ratio of exactly 9, so the gain is 10.0.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "Divided feedback"
sources.note: A divider in the feedback path gives a gain of 1 + Rfeedback/Rground with the same polarity as the input; the gain is never below 1 and reduces to the follower when the feedback resistor is zero; and the signal source supplies no current.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "Negative feedback"
sources.note: The voltage follower has a gain of 1 and a high input impedance, and its load current comes from the op amp's supply rather than from the signal source.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Operational Amplifiers" (last update 23 September 2026), section 3.10 "Inverting and noninverting amplification" (pp. 54–56)
sources.note: The closed-loop gain is the reciprocal of the feedback divider ratio, (RA + RB)/RB = 1 + RA/RB, found with zero input current and zero differential voltage.

templates.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier has Rf = {Rf} (output to inverting input) and Rg = {Rg} (inverting input to ground). The input is {Vin}. What is the output voltage?
templates.explanation: Rf and Rg form a divider from the output back to the inverting input, whose voltage must equal Vin. So Vout = Vin·(1 + Rf/Rg) = {Vin} × {G} = {answer}.
hints: The inverting input sees Vout through the Rf–Rg divider and must equal Vin.

misconceptions.feedback: You're missing the 1: a non-inverting gain is 1 + Rf/Rg, never less than 1.
That's the inverting amplifier. This one doesn't invert, and its gain is 1 + Rf/Rg.

steps: The golden rules make V− = V+ = {Vin}.
Rf and Rg form a divider from the output to V−, so V_out = V−·(1 + Rf/Rg).

followUps.prompt: Why is the gain 1 + Rf/Rg rather than Rf/Rg?

choices.text: The op amp drives the output until the divider Rf–Rg feeds back a voltage equal to Vin, so Vout = Vin·(Rf + Rg)/Rg
choices.feedback: Right: the divider hands back the fraction Rg/(Rf + Rg) of the output, and the op amp makes that equal to Vin.

choices.text: The extra 1 is the op amp's own gain added to the resistor gain
choices.feedback: The op amp's own gain is huge (around 100 000); the feedback divider, not the open-loop gain, sets the result.

choices.text: Current flows into the non-inverting input and adds to the output
choices.feedback: Ideal op-amp inputs draw no current.

choices.text: It isn't; the gain of a non-inverting amplifier is Rf/Rg
choices.feedback: That is the size of the inverting amplifier's gain. Here the input goes straight to the + input, so the output must be large enough that the divider returns all of Vin.

followUps.explanation: With negative feedback the op amp makes V− = V+ = Vin. V− comes from the divider: V− = Vout·Rg/(Rf + Rg). Solving gives Vout = Vin·(1 + Rf/Rg). Even with Rf = 0 the gain is 1, which is the voltage follower.

templates.prompt: You need a non-inverting amplifier with a gain of {G} using Rg = {Rg}. What value should Rf be?

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the 1 in G = 1 + Rf/Rg; your gain would come out one too high. Use Rf = (G − 1) · Rg.

followUps.prompt: Why can a non-inverting amplifier never have a gain below 1, whatever Rf and Rg you choose?

choices.text: The Rf–Rg divider returns at most all of the output to the − input, and that must equal Vin, so Vout ≥ Vin
choices.feedback: Right: V− = Vout·Rg/(Rf + Rg), a fraction no bigger than 1. For it to equal Vin, Vout must be at least Vin.

choices.text: It can: choose Rf smaller than Rg, and the gain drops below 1
choices.feedback: That works for the inverting amplifier (gain −Rf/Rin). Here Rf smaller than Rg gives a gain between 1 and 2, never below 1.

choices.text: The op amp's own gain adds 1 to whatever gain the resistors give
choices.feedback: The op amp's own gain is about 100 000, not 1. The 1 comes from the feedback divider, which returns only a fraction of the output.

choices.text: Current into the + input adds a copy of the input to the output
choices.feedback: An ideal op-amp input takes no current. The output is set by the feedback divider, not by input current.

followUps.explanation: Negative feedback makes V− = Vin, and V− comes from the output through a divider (from Foundations). A divider can only make a voltage smaller, so the output must be at least as big as the input. For a gain below 1, use a divider before the amplifier, or an inverting stage.

templates.prompt: A sensor with {Rs} output resistance must drive a {RL} load. Why put a voltage follower (unity-gain buffer) between them?

choices.text: Its input draws almost no current, so the sensor voltage isn't pulled down, and its output can drive the load
choices.feedback: Yes: high input resistance, low output resistance, gain of 1.

choices.text: It doubles the voltage so the load gets more
choices.feedback: A follower has a gain of exactly 1. Its value is in the impedances, not the gain.

choices.text: It inverts the signal so the load sees the right polarity
choices.feedback: A follower doesn't invert; the output follows the input.

choices.text: It isn't needed: {Rs} into {RL} works fine
choices.feedback: Connected directly, {Rs} and {RL} would form a divider, and most of the sensor voltage would be lost.

templates.explanation: Connected directly, {Rs} and {RL} would form a divider that would lose most of the signal. A follower has near-infinite input resistance (no loading) and near-zero output resistance (drives the load), with a gain of 1.

templates.prompt: Choose R_f and R_g (E24 values, 1 kΩ to 1 MΩ) for a non-inverting amplifier with a gain of {G}, within 5%.
templates.explanation: Gain = 1 + R_f/R_g, so R_f/R_g = {G} − 1. With R_g = 10 kΩ, R_f = {Rfex}; round to the nearest E24 value and recheck the gain. If neither neighbor is within 5%, change R_g instead: for example G = 15 → R_g = 3.3 kΩ, R_f = 47 kΩ (15.2); G = 18 → R_g = 3.0 kΩ, R_f = 51 kΩ (18.0); G = 20 → R_g = 4.7 kΩ, R_f = 91 kΩ (20.4).

templates.prompt: A voltage follower has a gain of exactly 1. Why is it still useful?

choices.text: It buffers: very high input resistance, very low output resistance
choices.feedback: Right: the source isn't loaded, and the output can drive a load the source couldn't.
Its gain is 1: the output voltage equals the input voltage.
A follower doesn't invert; the output follows the input.

choices.text: It removes the need for a power supply
choices.feedback: The op amp still needs supplies; the extra current comes from them.

templates.explanation: A follower copies the voltage but not the load: it draws almost nothing from the source and supplies the load current from its own supply. That isolates a weak source (a sensor, a divider) from a heavy load.
hints: Think about current, not voltage: who supplies the load current?
templates.noDrawing: why a unity-gain buffer is useful in general; no particular circuit

templates.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier has Rf = {Rf} (output to − input) and Rg = {Rg} (− input to ground). Rf is swapped for {new_Rf}, ten times bigger. What happens to the gain?

feedback.down: A bigger Rf makes the feedback divider hand back a smaller fraction of the output, so the op amp must drive the output higher to bring V− back up to Vin.
feedback.same: The gain is 1 + Rf/Rg, so it depends on Rf. A bigger Rf feeds back a smaller fraction of the output, and the output must rise to make up for it.

whatIf.factorHint: The gain is 1 + Rf/Rg. Only the Rf/Rg part grows with Rf; the 1 (the input itself) stays. Work out both terms before and after; there is no square or root in it.

templates.explanation: Gain = 1 + Rf/Rg goes from {before} to {after}: less than ten times, because only the Rf/Rg part grows tenfold, while the 1 stays. The 1 is the input itself: the output is always at least Vin, because V− has to reach Vin. The bigger Rf/Rg already is, the closer the change gets to ×10.
hints: Write the gain as 1 + Rf/Rg. Which part grows tenfold?

templates.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier (Rf = {Rf}, Rg = {Rg}, input {Vin}, op amp on ±15 V supplies, not drawn) drives a load RL = {RL}. RL is swapped for {new_RL}, a load ten times heavier. What happens to the output voltage?

feedback.down: That is what happens to a divider or a weak source when you load it. Here, if the output sagged, the divider would feed back less than Vin, and the op amp would push the output straight back up.
feedback.up: More load current can't push the output up: feedback keeps it where the divider returns exactly Vin.

templates.explanation: The output stays at Vin·(1 + Rf/Rg) = {after}. Feedback watches the output through the Rf–Rg divider: any sag would pull V− below Vin, and the op amp would raise its output until V− = Vin again. The load now draws {IL}, which comes from the op amp's supply. That is the low output resistance of a feedback amplifier (a real op amp manages this up to its current limit, typically about 20 mA).
hints: If the output sagged a little, what would happen to V−, and what would the op amp do?

templates.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier has Rf = {Rf} (output to inverting input) and Rg = {Rg} (inverting input to ground). What is its voltage gain?
templates.explanation: Feedback makes V− equal the input, and Rf and Rg divide the output down to V− by the fraction Rg/(Rf + Rg). So the output is the input divided by that fraction: gain = 1 + Rf/Rg = 1 + {Rf}/{Rg} = {answer}.
hints: V− must equal the input, and it sees the output through the Rf–Rg divider.

misconceptions.feedback: You're missing the 1. That's the size of the inverting amplifier's gain; the non-inverting gain is 1 + Rf/Rg, never below 1.
The ratio is upside down. Rf is the feedback resistor from the output: a bigger Rf means more gain, so the gain is 1 + Rf/Rg.
That's the fraction of the output fed back to V−. The gain is its reciprocal, (Rf + Rg)/Rg = 1 + Rf/Rg.

templates.prompt: This non-inverting amplifier runs from ±12 V supplies (rail-to-rail output, not drawn). With Rf = {Rf}, Rg = {Rg}, and {Vin} in, the output should be {h0}. The meter readings are below. Which fault explains them?

faults.text: Rf is open (cracked, or a dry joint)
faults.feedback: With Rf open, nothing would feed back from the output: Rg would hold the − input at 0 V, Rf would carry no current, and with the + input at {Vin} the op amp would drive its output to the +12 V rail.
faults.why: The output is at the +12 V rail, the − input reads 0 V, and Rf carries no current. Nothing reaches the − input from the output, so Rg holds it at ground. With V+ = {Vin} above V− = 0 V and no feedback, the op amp runs open loop and saturates high.

faults.feedback: With Rg open, the divider would have no path to ground: Rf would carry no current and drop nothing, so the − input would sit at the output voltage. Feedback would then make the output equal the input, {Vin}, with 0 A in Rf.
faults.why: The output equals the input and the − input reads the same voltage, yet Rf carries no current. With no path to ground, Rf drops nothing, so the whole output is fed back: the stage has become a voltage follower with a gain of 1. Rg's connection to ground is broken.

faults.text: Rf is shorted (a solder bridge across it)
faults.feedback: With Rf shorted, the output would be tied to the − input, so feedback would make the output equal the input, {Vin}. Rg would still carry its normal {Inorm} from the − input to ground, and that current would arrive through the bridge.
faults.why: The output equals the input, a follower, but the current through Rf's position is still the normal {Inorm}: Rg still pulls Vin/Rg from the − input, so the path to ground is intact. That current arrives without any voltage drop, so Rf is bridged.

faults.feedback: With Rg shorted, the − input would be tied to ground, so no output voltage could raise it to {Vin}. The op amp would drive its output to the +12 V rail, and Rf would carry 12 V/Rf = {Ishort} into the short.
faults.why: The output is at the +12 V rail and the − input reads 0 V, as if feedback were lost, but Rf carries {Ishort}, far more than normal: the feedback path is intact and its current goes straight to ground. The − input is shorted to ground, so the op amp can never pull it up to {Vin}, and it saturates trying.

templates.explanation: Compare the output with the input first. An output equal to the input means the stage has become a follower: the feedback divider returns all of the output, either because Rg's path to ground is gone (then Rf carries no current) or because Rf is bridged (then Rf's position still carries the normal Vin/Rg). An output at the +12 V rail means the − input can't reach Vin: it reads 0 V, either because nothing feeds back (Rf open, no current in it) or because the − input is shorted to ground (Rf then carries 12 V/Rf). The voltmeter readings alone can't separate them: Rf open and Rg shorted both put the output at the rail and the − input at 0 V. In every case, the current through Rf separates the two.
hints: Is the output still above the input, equal to it, or at a rail?
Then use the current through Rf: zero means the divider is broken; current means its path is intact.
